thread.title: Adding Walgreens to the Dow Is the Wrong Move

author: Andrew Bary
title: Adding Walgreens to the Dow Is the Wrong Move
text:
Photo: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images By Andrew Bary June 20, 2018 2:10 p.m. ET The Dow Jones Industrial Average got it half right in its latest shuffle.
The guardians of the index announced on Tuesday that they were booting General Electric (GE), with the change taking effect on June 26. But the Dow is light in new-economy companies, and the overseers missed an opportunity to address that when they decided to add Walgreens Boots Alliance (WBA) to the venerable 30-stock index rather than Facebook (FB) or another technology company.
Walgreens’ heyday was a decade or more ago, when drugstore chains were hot growth companies. Walgreens, whose shares are up 3%, to $67.67, in trading on Wednesday, is the 102nd largest company in the S&P 500 index, with a market value of $64 billion. It trades for a modest 11 times forward earnings, reflecting concerns about the impact of e-commerce on sales at the front of drugstores and the outlook for pharmacy sales.
Facebook , whose shares are up 2.6%, to $202.59, is the No. 5 company in the S&P 500, with a market value of $572 billion.
The five tech companies now in the Dow industrials are Apple (AAPL), which was added in 2015; Intel (INTC); IBM (IBM); Cisco Systems (CSCO); and Microsoft (MSFT). IBM has been among the worst Dow performers in recent years, while Intel and Cisco don’t have much impact on the index because they have relatively low prices. Cisco is trading around $44, and Intel, $53.
The Dow, which took its current form in 1896, is weighted by the stock prices of its components, not their market values.
The old-style price weighting probably has kept Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) and Amazon.com (AMZN) out of the index, because they would overwhelm the other components. Alphabet trades around $1,196, and Amazon, $1,758. The highest-priced stock now in the Dow is Boeing (BA), at $343.
S&P Dow Jones Indices, a unit of S&P Global, has been unwilling to include a high-priced stock at a fraction of its value, which might involve Alphabet or Amazon at 10% of their share prices. The index committee waited until Apple split its stock seven for one in 2014 before adding the iPhone maker to the Dow.
Another megacap stock that ought to get strong consideration for inclusion in the Dow is Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A), which now ranks sixth in the S&P 500, with a market value of $471 billion. The company’s Class B shares (BRK.B) now trade around $190. Other possible additions to the Dow include AbbVie (ABBV), Abbott Laboratories (ABT), Nvidia (NVDA), and Salesforce.com (CRM).
Newsletter Sign-up In announcing the change, S&P Dow Jones Indices said that “Walgreens is a national retail drugstore chain offering prescription and nonprescription drugs, related health services, and general goods. With its addition, the DJIA will be more representative of the consumer and health-care sectors of the U.S. economy. Today’s change to the DJIA will make the index a better measure of the economy and the stock market.”
A spokesman for S&P Dow Jones Indices declined to comment beyond its press release statement about the Walgreens addition.
GE’s deletion from the Dow wasn’t unexpected, given the sharp decline in its stock price, which has left it trading at $12.88, by far the lowest price among Dow components. GE accounts for less than one half of one percent of the index, making it largely irrelevant, given the index’s price weighting.
Corrections and Amplifications
The ticker for Alphabet is GOOGL. An earlier version of this article mistakenly listed it as AAPL.
